summary: Describes the security architecture needed to implement identity-based encryption, a public-key technology that uses a user's identity as a public key, and defines supporting data structures. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you need a special code key to send someone a secret. With this idea, their email address itself works as the key, so you can send a secret straight away. They get the matching key from a trusted server when they need it.

subtitle: How to build and run an identity-based encryption system.

tldr.problem: Ordinary public-key encryption needs the sender to hold the recipient's public key, which means publishing it, looking it up, or exchanging it in advance. All of that is work, and for a large set of users it is work nobody does.
tldr.mechanism: Identity-based encryption makes the public key computable from the user's identity and a set of public mathematical parameters. Two servers are needed: a Public Parameter Server that publishes the parameters, and a Private Key Generator that holds a master secret and computes private keys for users who authenticate to it.
tldr.outcome: The document is an Informational architecture and set of data structures. Encryption needs no server round trip once the parameters have been fetched, but the Private Key Generator becomes a single point of trust, because anyone who obtains its master secret can recreate every private key and decrypt every message.

today: RFC 5408 is an Informational document published in January 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an architecture and the data structures behind it: the algorithms themselves are in RFC 5091, and the use of the scheme for email is in RFC 5409.

sections.title: What Identity-Based Encryption Is
sections.content:
Identity-based encryption is a public-key encryption technology in which a public key can be calculated from an identity and a set of public mathematical parameters, and the corresponding private key can be calculated from that identity, those parameters, and a domain-wide secret value. Anyone with the public parameters can calculate an IBE public key, but a cryptographic secret is needed to calculate a private key, and only a trusted server holding that secret can do it.

The document describes the architecture of an IBE-based messaging system, how the components work together, and the data structures that support it. The objects are defined with ASN.1 and XML.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a randomly generated key that has to be handed out, the key is worked out from who you are. The public half can be worked out by anybody; the private half needs a secret that only a trusted server has.

sections.title: The Two Servers and the System Around Them
sections.content:
Two server components are required. The Public Parameter Server holds the publicly sharable cryptographic material, known as IBE public parameters, together with policy information for an associated private key generator, and provides a well-known location from which they can be distributed securely. The Private Key Generator stores and uses cryptographic material known as a master secret, which it uses to generate a user's IBE private key; it accepts a private key request and, after successfully authenticating the requester in some way, returns the private key.

A logical architecture would have one of each per name space, such as a DNS zone. The organisation controlling the zone would also control the servers, and therefore which of them to use when creating keys for its members, and the address of the public parameter server could be built from a user-friendly form of the identity it supports, for example an email address. That makes it clear which set of parameters to use and where to fetch them for a given identity.

Both the public and the private key can be calculated when needed, so keys are created just in time. That contrasts with other public-key systems, where keys are generated randomly and distributed before secure communication starts, and where private encryption keys have to be archived so they can be recovered if lost. Being able to calculate a recipient's public key in particular removes the need for the sender and the receiver to interact with each other, directly or through a proxy such as a directory server, before a secure message can be sent. One further characteristic distinguishes IBE from other server-based cryptographic systems: once a set of public parameters has been fetched, encryption is possible with no further communication with a server during the validity period of those parameters, whereas other server-based systems may need a connection to a server for every encryption operation.

IBE-encrypted messages can use standard message formats such as the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and IBE algorithms are used only for encryption, so digital signatures have to come from an additional mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Two servers do the work. One publishes the shared mathematical material that everybody needs, the other keeps the master secret and hands out private keys to people who prove who they are. A sensible design gives each organisation its own pair, usually one per DNS zone.

sections.title: Sending an Encrypted Message
sections.content:
To send an encrypted message, a user first obtains the recipient's public parameters, which may be available at a public parameter server operated by the recipient's organisation, by the sender's organisation, or by a different organisation entirely. The parameters contain everything the sender needs except the recipient's identity. The sender obtains them from a public parameter server at a well-known address, and the address from which they are fetched must be authenticated in some way: the servers must support TLS 1.2 or its successors. The sender selects the server and the corresponding key generator according to local security policy, since different servers may publish parameters for different algorithms or key strengths, or may require different levels of authentication before they hand out private keys.

With the parameters in hand, all that is needed to construct the message is the recipient's identity, whose form is defined by the parameters. When that identity is the same as the one a message would be addressed to, no more information is needed from a user to send an encrypted message than is needed to send an unencrypted one. That is one of the major benefits of an IBE-based messaging system. Identities can be individual, group or role identifiers.

To encrypt, the sender chooses a content-encryption key, uses it to encrypt the message, and then encrypts that content-encryption key with the recipient's IBE public key, as described in the Cryptographic Message Syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender fetches the shared material once, then needs nothing else but the recipient's address. Encrypting the message is the ordinary two-step: a random key encrypts the content, and the recipient's computable public key encrypts that random key.

sections.title: Receiving and Reading the Message
sections.content:
To read an IBE-encrypted message, the recipient parses it to find the address from which to obtain the public parameters needed for the calculations, and to find the part of the identity that was used to encrypt the message. The recipient then obtains the public parameters, which also give the address of the private key generator, and obtains the IBE private key from that generator after authenticating to it, receiving the key over a secure connection. The private key decrypts the content-encryption key, and that key decrypts the message.

Because the use of the correct public parameters is vital to the security of the system, they must be transported to recipients over a secure protocol, and users must check that the subject name in the server certificate matches the address of the public parameter server. The same applies to the private key: the servers must support TLS 1.2 or its successors, using the latest version supported by both parties, and the client must verify the server certificate and abort the request if verification fails, which protects the authentication credentials and the private key against man-in-the-middle attacks.

It may be useful for a private key generator to let users other than the intended recipient receive some private keys. Giving a mail-filtering appliance permission to obtain private keys on behalf of users, for example, lets the appliance decrypt and scan encrypted messages for viruses or other malicious features.

The private key request itself carries three things: the algorithm the key is wanted for, the identity it is wanted for, and the credentials of the person asking. The identity wanted may not be the one the credentials validate, for instance when a single user has access to several aliases such as two different email addresses. The request is an HTTP POST over a secure protocol, with an XML body naming the algorithm, the identity and any authentication data, and the reply is an XML response whose response code says what happened. The defined codes are IBE100 for success, with the private key in the body, IBE101 reserved, IBE201 to redirect the client to an external authentication mechanism, IBE300 for a system error, IBE301 for an invalid request, IBE303 for an obsolete client, and IBE304 for authorization denied. A client or server must support HTTP Basic authentication and should also support HTTP Digest authentication, and applications may use other means that suit them, such as an email application relying on deployed email infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The reader looks inside the message to find where the shared material lives, fetches it, then asks the key server for the private key, showing who they are. The server checks the certificate, checks the request, and either sends back the key or says no. A request that carries a wrong algorithm, an invalid request or a refused authorization gets its own distinct code.

sections.title: The Identity and the Public Parameters
sections.content:
The identity of a recipient is represented by a structure with four fields: a district, which is the address where the public parameters for that identity can be retrieved; a serial, an integer that distinguishes one set of parameters from another at the same district; an identity type, an object identifier saying how the identity data is encoded; and the identity data itself. Because the structure is used to calculate the keys, it is typically DER-encoded. What the identity actually contains depends on the application, so the document does not define an identity type that every application must support.

The public parameters are a structure with a version, which must be 2 for this format; a district name, which must be an encoding of a URI or IRI; a district serial, an integer identifying the set of parameters published at that name, which must be increased when new parameters are published; a validity period, with a not-before and a not-after time expressed in Greenwich Mean Time to the nearest second; the public parameters themselves, a sequence of algorithm identifiers with their parameter data; an identity type for the district; and optional extensions.

A client must check that the date on which it uses the parameters falls between the not-before and not-after times, and must not use them otherwise. The parameters must be regenerated and republished whenever the algorithm, identity type or extension values change, and a client should refetch them at a configurable interval. Where an identity carries a time component, that component must also fall inside the validity period. The parameters must identify at least one algorithm and must not repeat one; a client must implement the Boneh-Franklin algorithm and may implement others, and a client that supports none of the algorithms must fail with an error. Extensions may carry anything an implementation needs, such as a place where an encrypted message can be viewed by webmail users, or branding information so that a bank can present a different interface to different lines of business. A client that receives an extension it cannot process must not use the parameters for any cryptographic operation, and clients must be able to process parameters with no extensions at all. One extension is defined in the document: the address of the private key generator, whose presence obliges clients to use the private key request protocol with that address, and which should be present when the generator is publicly accessible so that private keys can be retrieved automatically.

Public parameters are fetched with an HTTP GET over a secure protocol, and the reply body holds the base64 encoding of the DER-encoded parameter structure, sent with the MIME type application/ibe-pp-data.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything has a version number, an expiry date and a serial number, so that a client can tell whether it is holding current parameters. The parameters say which algorithms are on offer and where the key server lives, and they can carry extra fields for whatever a particular deployment needs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attacks on the cryptographic algorithms themselves are outside the scope of the document, and are covered in the document that defines the algorithms, whose parameters give 80-bit, 112-bit and 128-bit encryption strength. The assumption is that capable administrators select parameters that give enough resistance to cryptanalytic attack.

Attacks that give an adversary access to or the ability to change the information on a public parameter or private key server, especially the master secret, defeat the security of the whole system: if the cryptographic material is compromised, the adversary can recreate any user's private key and therefore decrypt all the messages protected with the corresponding public key. The document therefore highly recommends that the ordinary physical and operational security practices be followed for these servers, that they be configured, sometimes called hardened, in line with best current practices, and that the system be operated in an environment where illicit access is infeasible. Attacks needing administrative access, or access equivalent to an IBE user, to the machines involved are also out of scope, as are attacks that need the administrators to be untrustworthy or the users to share their credentials.

The attacks that are in scope are those that let an adversary passively monitor information exchanged between users and the servers, masquerade as a public parameter or private key server, mount a denial-of-service attack on one of them, or easily guess a user's authentication credential.
sections.plainLanguage: The one thing that matters most is the master secret on the key server. If it leaks, everything encrypted with those parameters can be read, so the memo spends its warnings on protecting and hardening that server, and on the ways an attacker could still listen in or pretend to be the server.
